claim: Bees are capable of remarkable cognitive feats, particularly in visual learning.
source: Bees are capable of remarkable cognitive feats, particularly in visual learning (Chittka, 2022; Srinivasan, 2010; Turner, 1911; von Frisch, 1914; Wehner, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on bee visual learning capabilities.

claim: Bees can learn to associate a colour or orientation of a bar with reward.
source: They can not only learn to associate a colour or orientation of a bar with reward (Dyer et al., 2011; Guiraud et al., 2025b; MaBouDi et al., 2020b; Srinivasan, 1994; Stach et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies demonstrating associative learning in bees.

claim: Bees are able to identify specific features to categorise visual patterns by finding the relevant stimuli properties.
source: but are also able to identify specific features to categorise visual patterns, by finding the relevant stimuli properties (Benard et al., 2006; Guiraud et al., 2025a; Stach et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on bee pattern categorization abilities.

claim: Bees have demonstrated the capacity to grasp abstract concepts.
source: Furthermore, bees have demonstrated the capacity to grasp abstract concepts (Avarguès-Weber et al., 2011; Giurfa et al., 2001; Guiraud et al., 2018; MaBouDi et al., 2020c; Menzel, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research demonstrating abstract concept learning in bees.

claim: Bees can solve numerosity tasks by sequentially scanning the elements within a stimulus.
source: and solve numerosity tasks by sequentially scanning the elements within a stimulus (MaBouDi et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on bee numerosity abilities.

claim: It remains unclear how bees, despite their supposedly low visual acuity and limited neural resources, recognise complex patterns and perceive the intricacies of the natural world encountered during foraging.
source: Nevertheless, it remains unclear how bees, despite their supposedly low visual acuity (Gribakin, 1975; Spaethe and Chittka, 2003; Srinivasan and Lehrer, 1988) and limited neural resources, recognise complex patterns and perceive the intricacies of the natural world encountered during foraging (Chittka and Niven, 2009; Giurfa, 2013).
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap in understanding bee visual processing, supported by citations to studies on bee visual acuity and neural constraints.

claim: The natural scene that animals encounter is structured differently from random or artificial ones.
source: The natural scene that animals encounter is structured differently from random or artificial ones (Clark et al., 2014; Ruderman and Bialek, 1994; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on natural scene statistics.

claim: Visual sensory neurons evolve to exploit statistical regularities in natural scenes, efficiently encoding information through their spatiotemporal structures.
source: It has been hypothesised that visual sensory neurons evolve to exploit statistical regularities in natural scenes, efficiently encoding information through their spatiotemporal structures (Barlow, 1961).
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by a citation to Barlow's efficient coding hypothesis.

claim: Insect visual neurons have developed mechanisms that provide robust and efficient responses to naturalistic inputs.
source: Over evolutionary time, insect visual neurons have developed mechanisms that provide robust and efficient responses to naturalistic inputs (Dyakova et al., 2019; Dyakova et al., 2015; Dyakova and Nordström, 2017; Juusola et al., 2025; Song and Juusola, 2014; Zheng et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on insect visual neuron responses.

claim: Fly photoreceptors extract more information from naturalistic time series than from artificial stimuli or white noise, yielding stronger responses with a higher signal-to-noise ratio.
source: For instance, Song and Juusola, 2014 showed that fly photoreceptors extract more information from naturalistic time series than from artificial stimuli or white noise, yielding stronger responses with a higher signal-to-noise ratio (Song and Juusola, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a specific study on fly photoreceptor responses.

claim: Insect sensory pathways and their associated behaviours dynamically adapt to varying environmental conditions, adjusting their responses based on input parameters such as contrast, spatial frequency, and spatiotemporal correlations.
source: Additionally, numerous studies have demonstrated that insect sensory pathways and their associated behaviours dynamically adapt to varying environmental conditions, adjusting their responses based on input parameters such as contrast, spatial frequency, and spatiotemporal correlations (Arenz et al., 2017; Brinkworth and O'Carroll, 2009; Clark et al., 2014; Dyakova et al., 2019; Dyakova and Nordström, 2017; Juusola et al., 2025; Juusola and Song, 2017; Schwegmann et al., 2014; Serbe et al., 2016; Song and Juusola, 2014; Song and Juusola, 2014; van Hateren, 1997; van Hateren, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerous citations to studies on insect sensory adaptation.

claim: Experience-dependent adaptation has been observed in fly photoreceptors and motion-sensitive neurons in the lobula plate, enabling efficient visual processing under varying conditions.
source: Experience-dependent adaptation has been observed in fly photoreceptors and motion-sensitive neurons in the lobula plate, enabling efficient visual processing under varying conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the context of the paragraph and subsequent specific examples.

claim: Photoreceptors adapt their response dynamics to different light intensities, optimising sensitivity to natural stimuli.
source: For instance, photoreceptors adapt their response dynamics to different light intensities, optimising sensitivity to natural stimuli (Juusola and Hardie, 2001a; Juusola and Hardie, 2001b; Juusola and de Polavieja, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on photoreceptor adaptation.

claim: Motion-sensitive neurons such as the H1 neuron adjust their response properties based on prior motion exposure, enhancing motion detection in dynamic environments.
source: Similarly, motion-sensitive neurons such as the H1 neuron adjust their response properties based on prior motion exposure, enhancing motion detection in dynamic environments (Maddess et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on H1 neuron adaptation.

claim: Active sampling strategies—wherein animals actively scan their environment to extract visual information over time—are widely observed across species.
source: In animal vision, active sampling strategies—wherein animals actively scan their environment to extract visual information over time—are widely observed across species (Land, 1999; Land and Nilsson, 2012; Severance and Washburn, 1907; Varella et al., 2024; Washburn, 1908; Washburn, 1916; Yarbus, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on active vision across species.

claim: Primates employ eye movements, including saccades and microsaccades, to enhance fine spatial resolution and improve the encoding of natural stimuli.
source: Primates employ eye movements, including saccades and microsaccades, to enhance fine spatial resolution and improve the encoding of natural stimuli (Anderson et al., 2020; Land, 1999; Näher et al., 2023; Rucci et al., 2007; Rucci and Victor, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on primate eye movements.

claim: Insects utilise active vision strategies, incorporating characteristic head and body movements or specific approach trajectories to optimise visual processing during behavioural tasks.
source: Similarly, insects utilise active vision strategies, incorporating characteristic head and body movements or specific approach trajectories to optimise visual processing during behavioural tasks (Bertrand et al., 2021; Chittka and Skorupski, 2017; Dawkins and Woodington, 2000; Egelhaaf et al., 2009; Land, 1973; Land and Nilsson, 2012; Langridge et al., 2021; MaBouDi et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on insect active vision.

claim: Drosophila generate photomechanical photoreceptor microsaccades and can move their retinas to stabilise their retinal images, achieving hyperacute vision and enhancing depth perception.
source: Recent studies have shown that Drosophila generate photomechanical photoreceptor microsaccades and can move their retinas to stabilise their retinal images, achieving hyperacute vision and enhancing depth perception (Fenk et al., 2022; Hardie and Franze, 2012; Juusola et al., 2017; Kemppainen et al., 2022b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on Drosophila vision.

claim: Honeybee vision may require sequential sampling and integration of colour information due to their limited ability to discriminate between similar hues in brief flashes (<50 ms).
source: Likewise, honeybee vision may require sequential sampling and integration of colour information due to their limited ability to discriminate between similar hues in brief flashes (<50 ms) (Nityananda et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on honeybee colour discrimination.

claim: Bees engage in systematic scanning movements, continuously sampling their surroundings to construct an internal neural representation of their environment.
source: To overcome this constraint, bees engage in systematic scanning movements, continuously sampling their surroundings to construct an internal neural representation of their environment (Boeddeker et al., 2015; Collett et al., 1993; Doussot et al., 2020; Guiraud et al., 2018; Kemppainen et al., 2022a; Langridge et al., 2021; Lehrer and Collett, 1994; MaBouDi et al., 2020a; Werner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on bee scanning behaviour.

claim: Bumblebees enumerate visual elements sequentially rather than processing them in parallel, suggesting a reliance on scanning behaviour for feature extraction.
source: For instance, bumblebees enumerate visual elements sequentially rather than processing them in parallel, suggesting a reliance on scanning behaviour for feature extraction parallel (MaBouDi et al., 2020a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on bumblebee numerosity.

claim: Bumblebee flight trajectories indicate that they prioritise specific pattern regions before making a decision, rather than processing the entire pattern globally.
source: and their flight trajectories further indicate that they prioritise specific pattern regions before making a decision, rather than processing the entire pattern globally (Langridge et al., 2021; MaBouDi et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on bumblebee flight behaviour.

claim: The model extracts image input in five sequential patches of 75 × 75 pixels, sampled at a speed of 0.1 m/s, corresponding to a lateral displacement of 15 pixels between consecutive patches.
source: Building on findings from bee scanning behaviour (MaBouDi et al., 2025), the model extracts image input in five sequential patches of 75 × 75 pixels, sampled at a speed of 0.1 m/s, corresponding to a lateral displacement of 15 pixels between consecutive patches (Figure 1B; see Methods for details).
evidence: The claim describes the model's input parameters, supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The green pixel intensities of each patch modulate the membrane potentials of 5625 (75 × 75) grid photoreceptors within the simulated bee's single eye.
source: The green pixel intensities of each patch modulate the membrane potentials of 5625 (75 × 75) grid photoreceptors within the simulated bee's single eye.
evidence: The claim describes a specific aspect of the model architecture.

claim: Photoreceptor responses converge onto 625 lamina neurons via recurrent neural connectivity, providing a feedforward mechanism for transferring visual information.
source: These photoreceptor responses converge onto 625 lamina neurons via recurrent neural connectivity, providing a feedforward mechanism for transferring visual information.
evidence: The claim describes the model's neural connectivity structure.

claim: Lamina neurons project to 250 small-field medulla neurons through a simple feedforward pathway.
source: The lamina neurons then project to 250 small-field medulla neurons through a simple feedforward pathway (Figure 1C, see Methods).
evidence: The claim describes the model architecture, supported by reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Medulla neuron responses are progressively integrated into the synapses of their corresponding lobula neuron with a structured time delay.
source: For each of the five sequential patches that compose a full scan, medulla neuron responses are computed using a spiking neural model. These responses are progressively integrated into the synapses of their corresponding lobula neuron with a structured time delay.
evidence: The claim describes the temporal integration mechanism in the model.

claim: The synaptic weights dynamically encode the visual information at different temporal instances (T, 2T, 3T, 4T, and 5T), effectively aligning sequentially sampled spatial information into a temporally coherent representation.
source: As depicted in Figure 1D, the synaptic weights dynamically encode the visual information at different temporal instances (T, 2T, 3T, 4T, and 5T), effectively aligning sequentially sampled spatial information into a temporally coherent representation.
evidence: The claim describes the temporal coding mechanism, supported by reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Lateral inhibitory connections are proposed between lobula neurons to reduce correlation between them, enhancing redundancy reduction in the process.
source: Additionally, lateral inhibitory connections (red connections in Figure 1C) are proposed between lobula neurons to reduce correlation between them, enhancing redundancy reduction in the process.
evidence: The claim describes a model feature, supported by reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Connectivity in the medulla and lobula can be refined through exposure to sequences of time-varying images, incorporating non-associative learning rules and efficient coding principles.
source: We hypothesise that connectivity in the medulla and lobula can be refined through exposure to sequences of time-varying images, incorporating non-associative learning rules and efficient coding principles.
evidence: The claim presents a hypothesis about the model's learning mechanism.

claim: The receptive fields of lobula neurons exhibit spatiotemporal orientation selectivity after training on 100 flower and natural images (comprising 50,000 time-varying image patches).
source: Figure 2A illustrates the receptive fields of lobula neurons, which exhibit spatiotemporal orientation selectivity after training on 100 flower and natural images (comprising 50,000 time-varying image patches).
evidence: The claim describes results from the model, supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The receptive fields of lobula neurons are characterised by an elongated 'on' area (regions representing positive synaptic weights) adjacent to an antagonistic 'off' area (regions with negative synaptic weights).
source: The receptive fields of lobula neurons are characterised by an elongated 'on' area (regions representing positive synaptic weights) adjacent to an antagonistic 'off' area (regions with negative synaptic weights).
evidence: The claim describes the structure of receptive fields observed in the model.

claim: One lobula neuron responds most strongly to a 135° bar moving orthogonally to its 'on' or 'off' areas while exhibiting little or no response to other orientations.
source: For instance, one lobula neuron responds most strongly to a 135° bar moving orthogonally to its 'on' or 'off' areas while exhibiting little or no response to other orientations (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim describes a specific model result, supported by reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The population of 50 lobula neurons demonstrates specificity to both orientation and direction, closely resembling neuronal responses observed in bees and other insects.
source: The population of 50 lobula neurons demonstrates specificity to both orientation and direction, closely resembling neuronal responses observed in bees and other insects (James and Osorio, 1996; Paulk et al., 2008b; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013; Maddess and Yang, 1997).
evidence: The claim compares model results to biological observations, supported by citations.

claim: Only a small subset of lobula neurons respond at any given moment, indicating that their activity is decorrelated and relatively selective—an outcome of non-associative learning mechanisms in the visual lobe.
source: The results show that only a small subset of lobula neurons respond at any given moment, indicating that their activity is decorrelated and relatively selective—an outcome of non-associative learning mechanisms in the visual lobe (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim describes model results and attributes them to a specific mechanism.

claim: The two most active lobula neurons captured distinct structural features of the flower petal: one neuron's receptive field aligned with the left 45° edge of the petal, while another matched the right-angled edge.
source: Notably, the two most active lobula neurons captured distinct structural features of the flower petal: one neuron's receptive field aligned with the left 45° edge of the petal, while another matched the right-angled edge.
evidence: The claim describes specific model results demonstrating feature extraction.

claim: A representative lobula neuron tuned to a 150° orientation showed maximal firing (26 spikes/sec) when presented with a 150° moving bar.
source: To examine the selectivity of lobula neurons further, we analysed the spiking activity of a representative neuron tuned to a 150° orientation. As expected, the neuron showed maximal firing (26 spikes/sec) when presented with a 150° moving bar.
evidence: The claim describes a specific quantitative result from the model.

claim: The lobula neuron exhibited moderate responses to a horizontal bar and a 120° moving bar (18 spikes/sec) but remained largely unresponsive to other orientations.
source: It also exhibited moderate responses to a horizontal bar and a 120° moving bar (18 spikes/sec) but remained largely unresponsive to other orientations (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim describes model results, supported by reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The firing rate of lobula neurons increased with contrast at their preferred orientations, whereas responses to non-preferred orientations remained unchanged across contrast levels.
source: Consistent with experimental findings (Maddess and Yang, 1997), the firing rate of lobula neurons increased with contrast at their preferred orientations, whereas responses to non-preferred orientations remained unchanged across contrast levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim describes model results that match experimental findings, supported by citation and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Each lobula neuron responds maximally at a specific velocity, demonstrating a tuning curve that aligns with known insect neural responses.
source: Finally, Figure 2E highlights the velocity sensitivity of lobula neurons. Each neuron responds maximally at a specific velocity, demonstrating a tuning curve that aligns with known insect neural responses (Paulk et al., 2008b; Maddess and Yang, 1997).
evidence: The claim describes model results that align with biological observations, supported by citations and reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Training the non-associative learning model with a larger lobula neuronal population while maintaining the same underlying structure from photoreceptors to the medulla, enhances the diversity of orientation-selective responses.
source: Training the non-associative learning model with a larger lobula neuronal population while maintaining the same underlying structure from photoreceptors to the medulla, enhances the diversity of orientation-selective responses (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Video 2).
evidence: The claim describes model results with different parameters, supported by reference to supplementary figures.

claim: As the number of lobula neurons increases, their tuning properties become more distributed, enabling a finer and more precise encoding of different orientations and motion patterns.
source: As the number of lobula neurons increases, their tuning properties become more distributed, enabling a finer and more precise encoding of different orientations and motion patterns.
evidence: The claim describes an observed relationship in the model between neuron number and encoding precision.

claim: The correlation matrix of lobula neurons in response to 10,000 sequential scans of natural images after training reveals a highly decorrelated response pattern, with a strong diagonal structure indicating that each lobula neuron maintains a distinct response profile.
source: To assess the impact of training on the population activity of lobula neurons, we quantified their response sparsity and decorrelation before and after learning. Figure 3A presents the correlation matrix of lobula neurons in response to 10,000 sequential scans of natural images after training. The results reveal a highly decorrelated response pattern, with a strong diagonal structure indicating that each lobula neuron maintains a distinct response profile.
evidence: The claim describes quantitative results from the model, supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Before training, lobula neuron activity was broadly distributed, as reflected in the high sparseness index.
source: Before training, lobula neuron activity was broadly distributed, as reflected in the high sparseness index (see Methods).
evidence: The claim describes the initial state of the model before training.

claim: Training on natural images significantly reduced the sparseness index, indicating that lobula neurons developed a more selective and efficient coding scheme, where only a small subset of neurons responded to any given input.
source: Training on natural images significantly reduced the sparseness index, indicating that lobula neurons developed a more selective and efficient coding scheme, where only a small subset of neurons responded to any given input.
evidence: The claim describes the effect of training on the model, quantified by the sparseness index.

claim: Training on shuffled natural images led to only a moderate reduction in sparseness, suggesting that the implemented local synaptic plasticity rules alone are insufficient for optimal feature encoding without exposure to structured natural inputs.
source: In contrast, training on shuffled natural images led to only a moderate reduction in sparseness, suggesting that the implemented local synaptic plasticity rules alone are insufficient for optimal feature encoding without exposure to structured natural inputs.
evidence: The claim describes a control experiment result and its interpretation.

claim: Training on shuffled natural images results in non-structured receptive fields, leading to broadly distributed and less selective coding in the lobula neurons.
source: Notably, while shuffling natural images preserves pixel intensity and overall distribution, it disrupts spatial correlations and higher-order structures present in natural scenes. Consequently, training on these shuffled datasets results in non-structured receptive fields, leading to broadly distributed and less selective coding in the lobula neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim describes results from a control condition, supported by reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Following training, the MBON exhibited a distinct response pattern, with reduced activity towards the chosen visual stimulus and increased activity towards the rejected one.
source: After multiple training trials through a novel associative learning (see Methods and Discussion), the MBON exhibited a distinct response pattern, with reduced activity towards the chosen visual stimulus and increased activity towards the rejected one.
evidence: The claim describes the model's learning outcome after training.

claim: Simulated bees were trained to distinguish a plus sign from a multiplication sign, with training focused on the lower half of the plus pattern.
source: In the initial implementation, simulated bees were trained to distinguish a plus sign from a multiplication sign, with training focused on the lower half of the plus pattern (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup for the model, supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Following training, MBON activity decreased in response to the plus (S+) while increasing in response to the multiplication sign (S⁻), whereas prior to training, MBON responses to both patterns were similar.
source: Following training, MBON activity decreased in response to the plus (S+) while increasing in response to the multiplication sign (S⁻), whereas prior to training, MBON responses to both patterns were similar (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim describes the model's learning outcome, supported by reference to Figure 4B.

claim: A model with fixed, random connectivity in the visual lobe failed to differentiate between the plus and multiplication patterns.
source: In contrast, a model with fixed, random connectivity in the visual lobe failed to differentiate between the plus and multiplication patterns (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim describes results from a control condition, supported by reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Rewarding patterns elicited a reduction in extrinsic neuron responses, while punished patterns led to increased responses, a phenomenon consistent with neural activity recorded from alpha lobe PE1 neurons in the mushroom body.
source: Our model further revealed that rewarding patterns elicited a reduction in extrinsic neuron responses, while punished patterns led to increased responses (Figure 4B), a phenomenon consistent with neural activity recorded from alpha lobe PE1 neurons in the mushroom body (Okada et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim compares model results to biological observations, supported by citation and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: When the experimental conditions were adjusted so that simulated bees scanned only the lower half of the patterns or focused on the lower left corner, correct choice performance improved significantly, reaching ≥96% and ≥98%, respectively.
source: However, when the experimental conditions were adjusted so that simulated bees scanned only the lower half of the patterns or focused on the lower left corner—consistent with real bee behaviour (MaBouDi et al., 2021b)—correct choice performance improved significantly, reaching ≥96% and ≥98%, respectively (Figure 4C, first two pairs of bars).
evidence: The claim describes model performance under different scanning conditions, supported by citation and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing scanning speed (resulting in larger separations between sampled image patches) reduced accuracy to 70%, while stationary simulated bees—those that did not actively scan—achieved only 60% correct choices.
source: Conversely, increasing scanning speed (resulting in larger separations between sampled image patches) reduced accuracy to 70%, while stationary simulated bees—those that did not actively scan—achieved only 60% correct choices.
evidence: The claim describes model performance under different conditions.

claim: When the model bees were trained from a greater distance (>100 mm), they failed to discriminate between patterns.
source: In additional experiments where the model bees were trained from a greater distance (>100 mm), they failed to discriminate between patterns.
evidence: The claim describes model performance under a specific condition.

claim: Bumblebees approach stimuli to scan patterns at close range, and their initial approach choices are random.
source: Studies show that bumblebees approach stimuli to scan patterns at close range, and their initial approach choices are random (Guiraud et al., 2018; MaBouDi et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim describes bee behaviour, supported by citations.

claim: Different subsets of lobula neurons responded preferentially to the lower half of the stimulus, exhibiting stronger activation in a smaller neuronal subset.
source: The activity maps indicate that different subsets of lobula neurons responded preferentially to the lower half of the stimulus, exhibiting stronger activation in a smaller neuronal subset.
evidence: The claim describes model results comparing different scanning conditions.

claim: Scanning the entire pattern resulted in a more widespread and overlapping activation across the lobula neuron population.
source: In contrast, scanning the entire pattern resulted in a more widespread and overlapping activation across the lobula neuron population.
evidence: The claim describes model results for a different scanning condition.

claim: Neurons displayed stronger selectivity when scanning was restricted to the lower half at normal speed compared to whole-pattern scanning.
source: Corresponding spike rate plots (Figure 5, right panels) further highlight these differences, revealing that neurons displayed stronger selectivity when scanning was restricted to the lower half at normal speed compared to whole-pattern scanning.
evidence: The claim describes model results comparing scanning conditions, supported by reference to Figure 5.

claim: Neural responses exhibited a significantly larger angular distance when the model scanned only the lower half of the stimuli at normal speed compared to scanning the entirety of the same pattern.
source: The results (Figure 5C) indicate that neural responses exhibited a significantly larger angular distance when the model scanned only the lower half of the stimuli at normal speed compared to scanning the entirety of the same pattern.
evidence: The claim describes quantitative model results, supported by reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Simulated bees successfully discriminated between angled bars, a 22.5° angled cross from a 90° rotated version, and spiral patterns.
source: Our simulated bees successfully discriminated between angled bars (van Hateren et al., 1990), a 22.5° angled cross from a 90° rotated version (Srinivasan, 1994), and spiral patterns (Zhang and Horridge, 1992; Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim describes model performance on various tasks, supported by citations and reference to Figure 6A.

claim: When trained on grating patterns with –45° versus +45° orientations, the simulated bees successfully identified the correct pattern and demonstrated the ability to transfer the learned rule to novel patterns the model had never encountered during training, including single-bar patterns.
source: When trained on grating patterns with –45° versus +45° orientations, the simulated bees successfully identified the correct pattern. Moreover, it demonstrated the ability to transfer the learned rule to novel patterns the model had never encountered during training, including single-bar patterns (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim describes model performance demonstrating generalization, supported by reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The model exhibited a 22% lower preference for the negatively trained pattern compared to the novel pattern, validating the implementation of the rejection behaviour.
source: Notably, the model exhibited a 22% lower preference for the negatively trained pattern compared to the novel pattern, validating the implementation of the rejection behaviour and demonstrating that the model can simultaneously learn rewarding and aversive stimuli.
evidence: The claim describes a specific quantitative result from the model.

claim: The simulated bees discriminated training patterns containing two oriented bars in each lower quadrant with over 99% accuracy, but performance dropped to an average of 61% when presented with a simplified variant.
source: The simulated bees discriminated these training patterns with over 99% accuracy, but performance dropped to an average of 61% when presented with a simplified variant.
evidence: The claim describes model performance on a specific task.

claim: Simulated bees were able to identify the positive trained face from the negative one, as well as distinguish two novel faces and a caricature.
source: As with honeybees, our simulated bees were able to identify the positive trained face from the negative one, as well as distinguish two novel faces and a caricature.
evidence: The claim describes model performance on a facial recognition task, comparing to bee behaviour.

claim: Both the real and simulated bees failed to discriminate the faces when rotated through 180°.
source: Both the real and simulated bees failed to discriminate the faces when rotated through 180°.
evidence: The claim compares model and biological performance on a specific condition.

claim: The model failed to replicate the bees' ability to discriminate patterns from Stach et al., 2004, which require recognising the spatial arrangement of orientations across four quadrants.
source: The results indicate that the model failed to replicate the bees' ability to discriminate these patterns (Figure 6F), despite successfully distinguishing between the plus and multiplication signs when scanning the entire pattern (Figure 4C), even if its performance remained lower than that of real bees.
evidence: The claim describes a limitation of the model, supported by references to Figures 6F and 4C.

claim: Reducing the number of lobula neurons decreased the variability in their spatiotemporal receptive fields.
source: We found that reducing the number of lobula neurons decreased the variability in their spatiotemporal receptive (Figure 7A and Videos 3–5).
evidence: The claim describes model results with different parameters, supported by reference to Figure 7A and videos.

claim: When the network was limited to four neurons, it could not encode the full spatiotemporal structure of the training patterns obtained with the model with 50 lobula neurons—only vertical and horizontal receptive fields were produced.
source: In particular, when the network was limited to four neurons, it could not encode the full spatiotemporal structure of the training patterns obtained with the model with 50 lobula neurons—only vertical and horizontal receptive fields were produced (Videos 1 and 5).
evidence: The claim describes model results with a reduced number of neurons, supported by reference to videos.

claim: The overall performance of the model decreased as the number of lobula neurons was reduced.
source: As expected, the overall performance of the model decreased as the number of lobula neurons was reduced.
evidence: The claim describes a general trend in model performance.

claim: The model with 16 lobula neurons demonstrated the ability to discriminate more complex patterns beyond the plus and multiplication signs, but remained insufficient for recognising highly complex stimuli such as human faces.
source: Although the model with 16 lobula neurons demonstrated the ability to discriminate more complex patterns beyond the plus and multiplication signs (Figure 7B, C), it remained insufficient for recognising highly complex stimuli such as human faces (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: The claim describes model performance with a specific number of neurons, supported by references to figures.

claim: Fixed inhibitory connections limited the ability of the lobula neuron population to encode moving orientations.
source: These fixed inhibitory connections limited the ability of the lobula neuron population to encode moving orientations (Figure 8 and Video 6), indicating that the plasticity of inhibitory interneurons in the visual lobe plays a crucial role in facilitating an efficient representation of the visual environment.
evidence: The claim describes results from a control experiment, supported by references to Figure 8 and Video 6.

claim: The plasticity of inhibitory interneurons in the visual lobe plays a crucial role in facilitating an efficient representation of the visual environment.
source: indicating that the plasticity of inhibitory interneurons in the visual lobe plays a crucial role in facilitating an efficient representation of the visual environment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the control experiment results.

claim: Active scanning and non-associative learning dynamically shape neural activity, optimising information flow and representation.
source: Active scanning and non-associative learning dynamically shape neural activity, optimising information flow and representation.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the study.

claim: Lobula neurons, crucial for visual integration, self-organise into orientation-selective cells with sparse, decorrelated responses to orthogonal bar movements.
source: Lobula neurons, crucial for visual integration, self-organise into orientation-selective cells with sparse, decorrelated responses to orthogonal bar movements.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the study.

claim: Lobula neurons encode a range of orientations, biased by input speed and contrast, suggesting co-evolution with scanning behaviour to enhance visual representation and support efficient coding.
source: They encode a range of orientations, biased by input speed and contrast, suggesting co-evolution with scanning behaviour to enhance visual representation and support efficient coding.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings and offers an interpretation about co-evolution.

claim: The model demonstrates robust performance in pattern recognition, implying a similar encoding mechanism in insects.
source: The model demonstrates robust performance in pattern recognition, implying a similar encoding mechanism in insects.
evidence: The claim summarizes model performance and makes an inference about biological systems.

claim: The bumblebee has a pair of compound eyes that are composed of ~5500 ommatidia.
source: The bumblebee has a pair of compound eyes that are composed of ~5500 ommatidia (Spaethe and Chittka, 2003; Streinzer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is a biological fact supported by citations.

claim: Each eye contains three different types of photoreceptors, short, medium and long wavelength sensitive peaking in the UV, blue and the green, respectively.
source: Each eye contains three different types of photoreceptors, short, medium and long wavelength sensitive peaking in the UV, blue and the green, respectively (Menzel and Blakers, 1976; Skorupski et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is a biological fact supported by citations.

claim: The green photoreceptors are those that predominantly mediate visual pattern recognition.
source: Since the green photoreceptors are those that predominantly mediate visual pattern recognition (Giger and Srinivasan, 1996; Spaethe et al., 2001), we modelled that 75 × 75 green photoreceptors in one eye component are activated by the pixel values of the input pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and used to justify a modeling decision.

claim: The synaptic weights in the optic lobe were updated through exposure to natural images during the model's lateral scanning process.
source: The synaptic weights in the optic lobe were updated through exposure to natural images during the model's lateral scanning process (see Methods, Figure 1B).

claim: The model was trained using 50,000 time-varying image patches randomly sampled from a dataset of 100 natural flowers and scene images.
